overview: This bill directs the Treasury Department to push the World Bank, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, and other international development banks, which lend money to poorer and middle-income countries, to support nuclear power projects. U.S. representatives at those banks would advocate lifting bans on financing nuclear energy, as long as the technology meets standards common in the U.S. or allied countries, and building the banks' expertise to evaluate such projects. They would also push each bank to create a "Nuclear Energy Assistance Trust Fund" to offer competitive financing, including to counter loans from governments outside the main international export-credit agreement. The bill's findings point to Russia and China using reactor exports to gain long-term influence abroad. It requires yearly progress reports for seven years and expires after ten years. As of March 21, 2025, a House committee had approved it and it was placed on the House calendar.
for: Supporters say it helps countries get reliable, low-emission power from Western-standard reactors instead of relying on Russian or Chinese technology and financing.
against: Critics say nuclear projects are expensive, slow, and risky for developing countries, and steering development banks toward nuclear power could pull money away from cheaper or faster energy options.
